passages.text: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become highly effective for natural language understanding and generation; however, their reliance on static parametric memory makes them prone to hallucinations, outdated information, and unsupported factual claims, particularly in scientific and technical domains [9], [10]. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), introduced by Lewis et al. [12], addresses this limitation by coupling language models with external retrieval systems that provide dynamically retrieved evidence during generation. In a standard RAG pipeline, user queries are embedded into vector representations, relevant documents are retrieved from a vector store, and the retrieved context is incorporated into the model prompt for response generation. Although conceptually simple, the effectiveness of RAG systems heavily depends on retrieval quality, ranking strategies, query formulation, and context selection mechanisms [5, 7]. Recent work has proposed multiple enhancements to traditional retrieval pipelines, including query rewriting [14], hypothetical document generation [6], reranking approaches [16], reciprocal rank fusion methods [3], self-reflective retrieval systems such as Self-RAG [1], and agentic retrieval frameworks [15], [18], [19]. While these approaches improve retrieval quality and grounding, they also introduce additional computational cost and architectural complexity. Despite rapid progress in Retrieval-Augmented Generation research, practitioners still lack clear guidance regarding which retrieval strategies perform best under realistic deployment settings and large-scale scientific corpora. Existing studies often evaluate isolated retrieval components or rely on small benchmark datasets that may not reflect real-world scientific search environments.

This paper addresses these limitations by constructing a unified evaluation framework for comparing retrieval pipelines in scientific question answering systems. We evaluate six retrieval strategies: classic dense retrieval, LLM-based query rephrasing, query rephrasing with reranking, multi-query fusion using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), agentic retrieval, and late-interaction retrieval with ColBERTv2. All pipelines share a common corpus, generator model, and evaluation setup, and the five single-vector pipelines share a common embedding model and vector database, to ensure fair comparison. The contributions of this work are summarized as follows: 1. We construct a unified RAG evaluation framework over a large-scale corpus of scientific literature. 2. We compare six retrieval pipeline strategies under controlled experimental settings. 3. We release a synthetic scientific question-answering dataset generated from arXiv papers across multiple domains. 4. We analyze retrieval quality and response generation using LLM-as-a-judge evaluation methodologies and retrieval-oriented metrics. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on RAG systems and retrieval optimization techniques. Section 3 presents the methodology and retrieval pipelines, together with the datasets and evaluation setup. Section 4 reports experimental results and analysis. Section 5 discusses the findings, Section 6 outlines limitations, followed by conclusions in Section 7.

For each strategy we report results separately for the problem and method query subsets. We report (i) the answer rate — the percentage of queries with is_answer = true — and (ii) the mean of each 1–5 metric. By convention, zero-valued scores are excluded from the metric means, so per-metric averages reflect quality conditional on the model attempting an answer , while the answer rate captures how often it attempts one. We additionally report unconditional means, in which refusals remain as zeros, providing a single end-to-end score over all queries. All six strategies were run on the same 9,742 papers for which query generation succeeded, so each strategy has 19,484 question instances and every cross-strategy comparison is paired at the query level. Because every synthetic query has a known gold source paper, we also compute retrieval metrics directly from the run files: Hit@1 and Hit@3 measure whether the gold paper appears at those cutoffs, and MRR@3 rewards higher gold-paper rank.

Because every synthetic query has a known gold source paper, we can measure retrieval quality directly, independent of the judge. Table 5 reports gold-paper Hit@1, Hit@3, and MRR@3 per strategy and query type. ColBERT retrieves the gold paper within the top 3 for 92.8% of problem queries and 94.8% of method queries — roughly double the best single-vector pipeline (Rephrased & Reranked: 47.5% and 52.8%). Among the Chroma-based strategies the ordering broadly mirrors the judge scores: re-ranking improves over Classic, rewriting alone hurts retrieval on problem queries (Hit@3 39.7% vs. 46.3% for Classic), and Fusion is weakest. Retrieval quality translates directly into answer quality: conditioning on whether the gold paper was retrieved, the mean unconditional overall score is 0.36–1.18 points higher on gold-hit queries than on gold-miss queries for the Chroma-based strategies. Table 5: Gold-paper retrieval metrics by strategy and query type. RAG Strategy Query type Hit@1 (%) Hit@3 (%) MRR@3 (%) Classic problem 33.7 46.3 39.3 Classic method 35.7 46.8 40.6 Query Rephrased problem 28.3 39.7 33.3 Query Rephrased method 34.8 45.9 39.7 Rephrased&Reranked problem 36.7 47.5 41.6 Rephrased&Reranked method 44.3 52.8 48.2 Fusion problem 24.3 38.6 30.6 Fusion method 30.2 44.2 36.4 Tool Call problem 33.6 45.7 39.0 Tool Call method 37.5 48.5 42.4 ColBERT problem 86.5 92.8 89.4 ColBERT method 90.0 94.8 92.2

Figure 1 shows the per-metric average scores for each RAG strategy and query type. As shown, ColBERT RAG performed the best across nearly all metrics, followed by Rephrased & Reranked RAG; Fusion and Tool Call trail the Classic baseline. The relative performance stays consistent across the different metrics. Figure 2 shows the answer rate and overall answer quality for each RAG strategy and query type, confirming the conclusions above. Figure 3 shows gold-paper retrieval effectiveness per strategy, and Figure 4 shows the paired per-query effect of each strategy relative to Classic with 95% confidence intervals. Figure 1: The per-metric average score charts for each strategy: Classic RAG (baseline), Query Rephrased RAG, Rephrased & Reranked RAG, Fusion RAG (RRF), Tool Call RAG (agentic), ColBERT RAG (late-interaction). Figure 2: The Answer rate ( is_answer = true ) and Overall answer quality by query type (problem vs. method) and for each strategy: Classic RAG (baseline), Query Rephrased RAG, Rephrased & Reranked RAG, Fusion RAG (RRF), Tool Call RAG (agentic), ColBERT RAG (late-interaction). Figure 3: Gold-paper retrieval effectiveness (Hit@1, Hit@3, MRR@3) by strategy and query type. Figure 4: Mean paired per-query change in unconditional overall score relative to the Classic baseline, with 95% confidence intervals; positive values favor the named strategy.

The experimental results highlight the critical role of retrieval strategy selection in RAG pipelines. We observed that pipeline complexity does not linearly scale with retrieval performance. Among the single-vector strategies, the “Rephrased & Reranked RAG” approach achieved the highest overall scores (3.77/5), suggesting that model-based re-ranking effectively mitigates retrieval noise, while multi-query fusion and the agentic tool-call pipeline fell below the classic single-shot baseline (3.60/5) despite their additional LLM calls. This indicates that simpler architectures may offer cost-efficiency without significantly compromising performance. The clearest result, however, is the effect of the retrieval architecture itself. ColBERT’s late-interaction retrieval, indexed over the same full 463,971-paper corpus as the Chroma-based strategies, retrieved the gold paper in the top 3 for 92.8–94.8% of queries — roughly double the best single-vector pipeline — and produced the best answers on nearly every quality dimension (overall 3.94/5, paired delta + 0.37 +0.37 vs. Classic). Retrieval quality is linked to index composition, and comparisons of retriever architectures are unreliable unless all retrievers operate over the same document pool. The gold-hit analysis makes the mechanism explicit: conditional on retrieving the gold paper, all strategies produce answers of similar quality (overall ≈ \approx 3.8–4.0), so nearly all of the between-strategy differences are attributable to how often the right evidence reaches the generator, not to how the generator uses it.

passages.text: While Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) enables efficient task specialization, its learned updates can compromise capabilities beyond the target task. We identify adaptation imbalance : a few singular directions dominate the trained update, leaving its performance sensitive to how gains are allocated. We argue that learning where to adapt does not ensure that adaptation gains are well balanced . This motivates LoRA-Norm , a post-training normalization method that retains learned directions while rebalancing their gains. LoRA-Norm combines spectral rebalancing, a fixed nonlinear transformation of singular values, with nuclear-norm restoration, which preserves the original total spectral mass. It requires no calibration data or additional training and introduces no inference overhead. Across two backbones and three adaptation tasks, LoRA-Norm improves average specialization and capability retention, outperforming the evaluated post-hoc spectral pruning and gradient-guided editing configurations on both measures. Stronger functional equalization brings no consistent additional gains, revealing that balancing adapter gains and equalizing their responses are distinct objectives.

“The concern is not scarcity, but uneven distribution.” — Confucius, The Analects Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) specializes pretrained models by learning compact updates while keeping the original weights frozen ( Hu et al., 2021 ; Dettmers et al., 2023 ) . However, freezing pretrained parameters does not preserve pretrained behavior: the added update can improve the target task while compromising capabilities outside the adaptation distribution ( Shuttleworth et al., 2024 ) . This creates a practical challenge for deployment, where specialization and capability retention both matter ( Biderman et al., 2024 ) . An important question is whether a completed adapter can better satisfy these objectives through changes to how its learned directions are used. We examine this question by separating an adapter’s directions from their gains, building on a broader line of parameter-efficient methods that exploit weight decomposition or directional structure ( Meng et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Lingam et al., 2024 ) . The decomposition B ​ A = U ​ diag ⁡ ( σ ) ​ V ⊤ BA=U\operatorname{diag}(\sigma)V^{\top} expresses the update through learned singular directions and the strengths assigned to them. Although LoRA constrains the update rank, it does not require adaptation strength to be distributed evenly across these directions. Our measurements reveal substantial concentration in trained adapters, with directional output energy dominated by a small subset of the available components. We describe this uneven allocation as adaptation imbalance and investigate its deployment consequences by changing gains while keeping the learned directions fixed.

Our central argument is that learning where to adapt does not ensure that adaptation gains are well balanced . Training jointly determines directions and gains through a source-task objective, but the resulting configuration can remain improvable for specialization and broader capability retention. Prior work establishes the feasibility of post-training refinement through weight interpolation ( Wortsman et al., 2022 ) , spectral pruning ( Kumaravelu et al., 2026 ) , and calibration-gradient-guided reweighting ( Tian et al., 2026 ) . We investigate a simpler intervention: a fixed normalization rule that revisits the gains of a completed adapter using only its parameters. Figure 1: Learn the directions, normalize the gains. LoRA training learns useful adaptation directions, but the gains assigned to these directions can become imbalanced. LoRA-Norm keeps the learned directions fixed and rebalances only their gains after training, improving specialization while preserving capabilities beyond the target task. We propose LoRA-Norm , which combines spectral rebalancing with nuclear-norm restoration , as shown in Fig. 1 . Spectral rebalancing applies a short, fixed sequence of nonlinear transformations to the singular values while preserving their associated directions. Nuclear-norm restoration rescales the transformed gains to preserve their original sum within each module. This changes the allocation of spectral mass without requiring an exactly flat spectrum. The edited update is reconstructed as standard low-rank factors with the original adapter configuration and scaling. LoRA-Norm therefore requires no calibration data or additional training and introduces no inference overhead.

We evaluate 18 trained adapters spanning two backbones and three adaptation tasks in coding, mathematical reasoning, and instruction following. LoRA-Norm improves average target-task performance and capability retention, exceeding the evaluated spectral-pruning and gradient-guided editing configurations on both measures. These results show that the same learned directions can support better deployment performance after gain normalization, without any additional training. Our analysis also clarifies what this improvement means. Preserving nuclear norm does not preserve update magnitude, and a direction’s functional contribution depends on both its gain and the inputs that activate it ( Paischer et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) . Controls matched to LoRA-Norm’s activation-weighted update energy recover much of its benefit, while stronger functional equalization provides no consistent additional gains. Thus, balancing adapter gains and equalizing their responses are distinct objectives . Directional concentration is useful for characterizing an adapter, but uniformity alone is insufficient to judge whether an edit improves specialization and retention. In a nutshell, our contributions are summarized as follows: • Empirical insight. We characterize adaptation imbalance in trained LoRA adapters and show that their learned directions can support improved specialization and capability retention through post-training gain adjustment. • Practical method. We introduce LoRA-Norm, a fixed spectral normalization procedure that preserves learned directions and per-module nuclear mass, requiring neither calibration data nor additional training or inference operations.

• Functional analysis. We examine gain redistribution alongside update strength through matched-strength controls and activation-aware interventions, showing why stronger response equalization is not a reliable objective for adapter refinement.

Our results show that the same learned adaptation directions can support better specialization and capability retention after gain adjustment. LoRA-Norm revisits this allocation through fixed spectral rebalancing and per-module nuclear-norm restoration, without calibration data, retraining, or inference overhead. Across 18 adapters spanning two backbones and three tasks, it improves both objectives on average. Energy-matched controls recover much of the benefit, while stronger functional equalization yields no consistent further gains, limiting claims of an independent spectral-shape advantage. Thus, balancing adapter gains and equalizing functional responses are distinct objectives. Broader model and task coverage and further controlled replications would help assess generality.

decision.reason: Seven well-supported papers cover the main research goals. Remaining uncertainty includes transfer from idealized spectral models to LLM pretraining and reproducibility of reported gains; further available actions are unlikely to change this selection.

selections.summary: Learnable Subspace Projections optimizes compression subspaces end-to-end while freezing pretrained weights. At 70% compression on Llama-2-7B, it reports 10.9 WikiText-2 perplexity and 42.2% mean zero-shot accuracy, versus 13.3 and 36.0% for its strongest baseline.
selections.relevance: Directly informs how to preserve model quality under low-rank weight compression, though it does not train weights to become more compressible.

evidence.quote: we optimize all projectors jointly across the network with the pretrained weights frozen.
At − 70 % -70\% compression, LSP brings Llama-2-7B to 10.9 10.9 WikiText-2 perplexity and 42.2 % 42.2\% mean zero-shot accuracy, versus 13.3 13.3 and 36.0 % 36.0\% for the strongest baseline.

selections.summary: Derives how optimizer geometry changes singular-mode emergence and decay in deep matrix factorization. Controlled experiments show different transient rank trajectories even when optimizers reach similar final losses and effective ranks.
selections.relevance: Addresses whether optimization changes effective rank, but its phase laws rely on balance and alignment assumptions rather than LLM experiments.

evidence.quote: Although the methods eventually reach similar losses and effective ranks, their trajectories differ substantially.
Although the phase laws rely on balance and alignment assumptions, they identify concrete mechanisms to understand optimizer behavior.

selections.summary: Uses seed-paired, module-matched rank sweeps to study LoRA under label noise. On Qwen2.5-7B with 20% noise, the measured LoRA ranks remain worse than dense fine-tuning of the same modules, despite a second descent relative to the earlier LoRA peak.
selections.relevance: Connects LoRA rank, memorization and generalization under label noise, with a direct language-model test.

evidence.quote: we repeat the measurement on Qwen2.5-7B ( Qwen Team, 2024 ) over 5,000 5{,}000 AG News examples ( Zhang et al., 2015 ) with 20 % 20\% label noise
G G remains positive at every measured rank and in every seed, parity included.

selections.summary: Clean sketches two-sided curvature preconditioners; Q-Clean compresses optimizer states further. At LLaMA-1.3B, Q-Clean reports 1.28G optimizer memory and 12.10 perplexity versus Muon's 2.80G and 11.78. Clean reports reaching AdamW's final loss in 64 rather than 81 hours on four H100 GPUs.
selections.relevance: Provides measured memory, quality and wall-clock tradeoffs for memory-efficient LLM pretraining.

evidence.quote: Clean reaches AdamW’s final performance in 64 hours instead of 81

selections.summary: RoM optimizes LoRA updates on a fixed-rank manifold to account for factorization gauge symmetry. In a three-run Qwen2.5-3B RL comparison, it reports higher accuracy than Adam on MATH-500, GSM8K and OlympiadBench, with 1.08× end-to-end time per step.
selections.relevance: Directly addresses low-rank optimization geometry and practical language-model fine-tuning.

evidence.quote: We design our optimizer on the manifold of fixed-rank matrices, aiming to optimize the product of the low-rank factors directly rather than each factor separately.

selections.summary: LoRA-Norm rebalances an adapter's singular-value gains after training while preserving per-module nuclear norm. Across 18 adapters, it reports average improvements in specialization and capability retention; energy-matched controls recover much of the benefit.
selections.relevance: Tests a spectral intervention on LoRA updates, while cautioning against attributing its gains solely to spectral shape.

evidence.quote: Across 18 adapters spanning two backbones and three tasks, it improves both objectives on average.
Energy-matched controls recover much of the benefit, while stronger functional equalization yields no consistent further gains, limiting claims of an independent spectral-shape advantage.

selections.summary: Compares six retrieval strategies on a shared scientific-paper corpus and synthetic question set. ColBERT reports gold-paper Hit@3 of 92.8–94.8%, versus 47.5–52.8% for rephrasing plus reranking.
selections.relevance: Directly informs retrieval and ranking choices for a research-digest agent; the synthetic queries limit direct transfer to personalized paper selection.

evidence.quote: All six strategies were run on the same 9,742 papers for which query generation succeeded, so each strategy has 19,484 question instances and every cross-strategy comparison is paired at the query level.
